At 3:40 a.m., while the second batch of rye was proofing, Marisol found it again: a library book on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley.

Fourth Thursday running. Same book, *A Field Guide to Night Birds*, stamped Eastgate Branch and due three weeks ago. Each time, she'd carried it to the drop box on her way home. Each Thursday it came back, as if the building itself had borrowed it.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A folded index card slid out from the page on barn owls.

*You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog then, because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. —R.*

Marisol read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, the fan hummed, pushing warm air into the dark.

She turned the card over. With the grease pencil she used for marking trays, she wrote: *Rye's out at 4:15.* Then she tore a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, set the book on top, and propped the back door open one inch.

Thursdays, the book shows up. Not on the counter, mind you, but wedged behind the flour bins by the back door, like whoever leaves it knows exactly where I won't trip over it.

It's always the same one: *A Field Guide to North American Moths*, Elmwood Branch, due date stamped so long ago the ink's gone violet. I've never seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow-deep in rye dough by two, and honestly, at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band.

The first few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register. By Friday morning it was gone. Thursday, back again. Fine. People are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter, so I'm not judging.

Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths.

*They only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone?*

No signature. Just pencil, pressed hard.

I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper, and set it behind the flour bins.

At 2:40 the proofing cabinet clicked off, and Dana went to the back door for the milk crates. The book was on top of them again, in a bread bag knotted at the neck.

Fourth Thursday. Same book: a water-stained copy of *Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest*, property of the Alder Street branch, due date stamped in purple twelve years ago. The first time, she'd put it in the lost-and-found bin. The second time, she'd driven it to the library's return slot. It came back anyway, on the crates, before dawn.

Tonight a square of lined paper stuck out of chapter six, near the photograph of a chanterelle.

*You open at 6. They open at 10. I can't wait that long. Can you give it to Marguerite at the desk? Tell her I didn't pick the wrong ones.*

No name. The handwriting leaned hard to the right, like it was walking into wind.

Dana read it twice, then set the book on the shelf above the flour bins, where nothing got wet. She pulled a pencil from behind her ear, turned the note over, and wrote: *Which ones did you pick?* She tucked it back into chapter six and left the bread bag on the crates, open.

At 3:40 a.m., while the second batch of rye proofed, Marisol found it again: a library book on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley.

Fourth Thursday running. Same book, *A Field Guide to Night Birds*, Eastgate Branch, with a fresh due-date slip every time. She'd dropped it in the return box on her way home each week, and by the following Thursday someone had checked it out again and carried it back here.

She scraped dough from her knuckles and opened it. A folded index card slid out from the page on barn owls, where someone had penciled a check beside *call: a long, harsh scream*.

*You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog at half past three, because she can't anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking this out again. —R.*

Marisol read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, the fan rattled steam across the wet dumpster lid.

She turned the card over. With the grease pencil she used for marking trays, she wrote: *Rye's out at 4:15.* Then she wrapped a heel from yesterday's loaf in wax paper, set it on the outside step, laid the book on top, and propped the back door open one inch.
